As is well known, higher interest rates are poison for precious metals, cryptocurrencies, and riskier investments. This also includes the AI and quantum sectors. Nevertheless, evidence continues to mount that we could be marking a medium-term low these days. Several sentiment indicators are signaling that the market has now gone too far. And once sentiment hits rock bottom, a strong rebound is often not far off.

You probably remember the fractal chart we presented in the Thoughts from September 2, 2026. It compares the current performance of the S&P 500 with that from 1995 onward, when the dot-com bubble began—right up to its inglorious end. The theory behind fractal charts is that investors consistently react in similar ways in comparable situations. And lo and behold: to this day, this chart shows an almost uncanny correlation of +0.99. If history were to repeat itself, a serious correction wouldn’t begin until next spring.

But if the stock market were that simple, we could all just sit back and relax. As we know, fractal charts only work until they stop working. The following fractal chart—which we’re showing here for the first time—also displays an impressive correlation of +0.93. But it tells a completely different story: According to this chart, the Nasdaq is currently merely undergoing a sharp correction before that much-cited bubble really starts to inflate next year…

So we have no choice but to take a closer look at the short- and long-term outlook—especially developments in the AI sector. In the issue from September 2, we already discussed that our margin call indicator had generated a sell signal. The subsequent correction did indeed lead to forced selling, particularly among AI stocks. The recent price slide and the associated drop in sentiment could now tempt some investors to prematurely write off AI and draw parallels to the dot-com bubble.

But people tend to forget just how crazy the party actually was back then. At the height of the dot-com bubble, all it took was to include the magic word “Internet” in a business plan, and a billion-dollar valuation was within reach. Investors poured money in and cheered, stocks soared—and the imagination knew no bounds.

With the so-called “AI bubble,” however, the situation is fundamentally different. This time, it’s not primarily euphoric investors driving stock prices to dizzying heights. Rather, it’s the management teams of the world’s largest IT conglomerates who apparently see a massive risk in missing out on a technological revolution without making massive investments.

Of course, one can debate whether all the CEOs of these trillion-dollar corporations have collectively succumbed to naivety. We find that hard to believe. After all, AI will fundamentally transform nearly every industry in the coming years—and in some cases, it already is. To put it even more plainly: The technological revolution has long since become a strategic race between the two greatest powers on our planet—the U.S. and China. This is about far more than chatbots and data centers. AI will also influence the balance of political power and give the frontrunner additional advantages.

And in this race of all races, the U.S. has just taken its quarterback off the field. It remains to be seen whether the game can be won without him. The media is focusing on the allegations of sexual misconduct. As is well known, Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos, and Elon Musk have also made headlines for similar reasons—to name just a few prominent figures. But perhaps there is more to the rumors surrounding the dispute between open-source and closed-source AI. Without reliable sources, however, this remains speculation. What is undisputed, however, is that companies’ appetite for investment shows no signs of abating for the time being. Goldman Sachs estimates that annualized U.S. AI investments could swell to a staggering $1.4 trillion by the end of 2027. So there’s hardly any sign of a sudden slowdown.

And while the investment machine continues to run at full speed, the stocks of some affected companies have become surprisingly cheap following the correction of the past few weeks. Another significant difference from the dot-com bubble: About 30 years ago, very few of the market darlings of the time had any significant cash flow to speak of. Today, the financial situation of many AI heavyweights looks quite different.

Many investors instinctively turn to the price-to-earnings ratio (P/E ratio) when valuing stocks. But especially when debt plays a significant role, it’s worth taking a look at the EV/EBITDA ratio. Enterprise value (EV) takes into account not only a company’s market capitalization but also its net debt. Put simply, the EV/EBITDA ratio shows how many years of current operating profit before depreciation and amortization the total company valuation corresponds to—assuming EBITDA remains constant. For most companies, however, this figure is likely to rise in the coming years. The following chart shows the trend of this metric for five selected market leaders over the past two years. And lo and behold: with one exception, there hasn’t been much room to pull back on valuations lately.

P/E ratios, on the other hand, have—and how! Nvidia wasn’t last valued this cheaply back in 2019. Who would have thought …

Even compared to other companies in the IT sector, valuations now appear attractive. However, one shouldn’t automatically interpret this as a buy signal. After all, every company writes its own growth story.

Back to market developments: The pendulum of sentiment has now swung with full force to the other side. As recently as this spring, the Nasdaq Index was marked by almost fearless optimism. Today, however, pessimism seems to be booming. From euphoria to despair—the stock market is, after all, a stage for grand drama.

But while the masses are still grappling with their fears, savvy investors behind the scenes have already begun to take advantage of the price weakness to accumulate positions. Our Smart Investors Action Indicator shows, via the orange trend line, that the tide has now turned.

Over the past few weeks, many investors have sought refuge primarily in defensive stocks. But this urge for safety is now losing steam—another bullish sign. Apparently, capital is slowly venturing out of its safe haven again.

“Buy the Fear” thus remains the preferred motto. Whether, on the other hand, we are actually facing the end of the great bull market in the long term remains to be seen. In the short and medium term, however, the pendulum seems to have swung so far south that a strong move back toward the north is becoming increasingly likely.

Things also remain exciting with gold and cryptocurrencies, whose developments continue to follow our script with astonishing precision. Fears about interest rates are making life difficult for them. But more on that in the insights of the next issue.

data.title: Dow Jones Industrial Average Drops As UnitedHealth And Nvidia Fall

Chair Harvey Jones told the earnings call the board doesn't intend to bring back former chief executive Jensen Huang. Anthropic (ANT) starts trading on Nasdaq on Thursday at a reported $83 a share, above its $70-$78 range, and index member Amazon (AMZN), an investor in it, rose about 4%.

The Fed minutes didn’t appear to play any meaningful role in today’s implied volatility moves.

The S&P 500 is sitting on the put wall at 7,300, which is an important support level right now. It would likely take a gap down to push the index below that level, and with monthly options expiration on Friday, I’m not convinced a break of support is likely just yet.

The put wall at $150 held for Nvidia (NVDA) today, and if those puts aren’t monetized soon, we could see the stock snap higher again, even if the move is purely mechanical in nature.

Gold is also breaking support, falling 3% today and now trading around $3,700. At this point, it is starting to look oversold, with the price reaching its lower Bollinger Band and the RSI dipping below 30. A bounce or a period of sideways consolidation seems likely to follow. Whether gold eventually moves even lower will depend on how much further the dollar strengthens and interest rates rise, even if that decline doesn’t happen immediately.

Silver fell by about 5% today, breaking below support around $46.50. It is also approaching oversold conditions, and I wouldn’t be surprised to see the decline pause.

One reason gold and silver are getting crushed is that the dollar continues to strengthen. Unfortunately for both metals, I think the Dollar Index has room to move even higher, potentially returning to around 104.75.

Bitcoin (BTC.X) fell another 4% today and is now sitting on support around $63,000. Tomorrow, another $14.2 billion in T-bills will settle, followed by $51.3 billion on Tuesday, November 24. At this point, I still think there is room for Bitcoin to move lower, potentially heading toward the low-$50,000 range.

data.title: High Expectations Of Delayed Home Ownership
data.description:
For the past two years, the housing narrative has been dominated by a single number: the thirty-year mortgage rate. With rates remaining high relative to pandemic-era lows, consensus expectations imply homebuilding is a cyclical business in retreat, waiting for the Federal Reserve to rescue it. In many ways, this view is understandable. A buyer who locked in a low rate is reluctant to sell, and a buyer shopping today faces a payment that looks unforgiving next to the one her neighbor enjoys. Put differently, the market has spent its energy debating the price of money and very little asking who is forming households, and what, precisely, they are willing to buy.

For more than a decade following the Great Financial Crisis, the United States built fewer homes than its population growth, household formation, and aging housing stock required. Builders and their lenders had been scarred by the bust, and land developers were wiped out in great numbers. Housing starts recovered slowly and remain below trend growth today. A shortage of this kind does not disappear because the mortgage rate fluctuates in a given quarter; it is cured only by construction, and construction is being constrained by the same high rates that frighten investors.

The demand side is where we have variant perceptions. While the affordability problem is real: rates, taxes, insurance, and down payments have made ownership expensive for many lower- and middle-income households, we observe the narrower cohort of married, college-educated, dual-income couples without children, who have adequate credit and income yet remain renters for partially non-economic reasons. Many of them will pay as much each month for a small city-center apartment as a suburban mortgage would cost at 6-7% rates and still decline the house. The decision is not rent versus buy. It is a walkable, flexible, experience-rich life versus a suburban or exurban home surrounded by identical structures, a Target (TGT) Supercenter, a Home Depot (HD), and perhaps even a Buc-ee’s. Put in those terms, the rent is not the obstacle; the trade is.

Large builders solve affordability with cheap land and a standardized product. This manufacturing assembly line produces a product that is spacious, with spare bedrooms, a yard, and a two-car garage space. What the buyer surrenders is time, since a longer commute works as an implicit mortgage attached to the cheaper house, walkability, and identity, since the standardized subdivision offers little of it. For a childless couple, the extra bedrooms and the school district are excess capacity, a payment today for a contingent future use. The apartment’s rewards are immediate and visible; the house’s are deferred and conditional. Adding children on top of this is another expense that conflicts directly with their budget for (yet another) trip to Tuscany.

There is also a psychological element, one that we believe social media has amplified. Prior generations measured their standard of living against relatives, coworkers, and the neighbors visible from the front porch. Today’s young adults measure theirs against an algorithm that overweights the exceptional: the best restaurant, the renovated kitchen, the vacation, the promotion. They compare those highlights with their own complete budget, commute, and ordinary weekdays, while the hidden inputs of parental help and “sponsorship” go unseen. Researchers such as Juliet Schor, Ethan Kross, and Philippe Verduyn have documented how reference groups and passive scrolling breed upward comparison and envy. Vacations are photogenic and rewarded with attention; the joys of home ownership as defined by property taxes, insurance, and HVAC replacements are not. Keeping up appearances means immediate gratification, while the long-run gains of ownership appear nearly invisible.

This creates a coordination problem the market under-appreciates, because houses and children are complements. A couple says it will buy when it is ready for children, and that it will have children once it is settled in the right house, and the apartment-and-delay equilibrium can persist for years. We believe shifting lifestyle choices therefore postpone household formation rather than abolish it altogether. The $64,000 question is if many of these couples will eventually buy when children arrive, when travel and “big dumb lines” lose their marginal appeal.

NVR (NVR), D.R. Horton (DHI), and Lennar (LEN) share a characteristic that is easy to overlook in a debate about rates: each has changed the way it does business. NVR has long favored lot options over owning large amounts of land, keeping its capital employed low and its returns high. D.R. Horton has paired its scale and inventory discipline with a growing rental and lot-development business that diversifies its earnings. Lennar has also moved towards a land-light model, and is making the boldest bet on a housing start recovery by keeping volumes constant at the expense of near-term profitability. Each path differs slightly, but we believe each leads to a business that earns more per dollar invested and is far less vulnerable to the land write-downs that devastated the industry in the 2008 financial crisis.

The balance sheets tell the same story. The homebuilders of the last cycle entered the downturn burdened with debt and overpriced land, and many did not survive it. Today, the three companies we own carry modest leverage, hold substantial liquidity, and continue to repurchase shares at what we believe are attractive prices. In many ways, a company that can use a period of high rates to buy back stock, take share from weaker competitors, and secure land on favorable terms is being strengthened by the very conditions that are causing the industry to be shunned by investors today.

Housing starts may or may not return to trend, the birth rate may or may not recover, and mortgage rates may or may not decline. Regardless of these outcomes, we believe the through-cycle margins, the return on capital, and the balance sheet strength of NVR (NVR), D.R. Horton (DHI), and Lennar (LEN) are improving. In a market fixated on the price of money, we prefer to own the companies that are laser-focused on per-share value creation regardless of the state of the yield curve or the latest viral trend.
